entities.summary:
Montreal is the largest city in the province of Quebec, the second-largest city in Canada, and one of the major urban centers of North America. Founded in 1642 as Ville-Marie — a utopian Christian mission by Paul Chomedey de Maisonneuve — it has grown into a bilingual metropolis of 4.3 million people that is the cultural, commercial, and intellectual capital of French Canada.

The island of Montreal at the confluence of the St. Lawrence and Ottawa rivers was a significant Indigenous meeting place (the Hochelaga village visited by Jacques Cartier in 1535) long before French colonization. The fur trade made Montreal the economic engine of New France — the gateway through which North American furs reached European markets from the 1640s onward. The British conquest of New France (1760) and the Treaty of Paris (1763) transferred Montreal to British control, creating the cultural tension between French and English Canada that has defined the city ever since.

Montreal was Canada's largest city from the mid-18th century until Toronto surpassed it in the early 1970s. The city hosted Expo 67 (World's Fair, 1967) and the Summer Olympics (1976), both transformative events for the city's self-image. The rise of Quebec separatism in the 1970s–1980s drove English-speaking corporations and institutions to Toronto, reshaping the Canadian economic geography. Today Montreal is an international hub for aerospace, AI and technology, film, music, and gaming — and its bilingual French-English culture is a distinctive North American phenomenon.
